name: Cairo
info: Cairo is the capital of Egypt, on the Nile where the valley opens into the Delta. The Fatimids founded it in 969 beside the older settlement of Fustat, and it has been Egypt's main city ever since.

facts.founded: 969, when the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah had his general Jawhar al-Saqili build a new fortified city northeast of Fustat; the caliph arrived in 973 and gave it its name
facts.where: On the east bank of the Nile and two islands in it, just south of the point where the river leaves its desert valley and branches into the Delta, in northern Egypt
facts.known: Fustat and the Fatimid foundation of al-Qahira; al-Azhar; Saladin's Citadel; the Mamluk sultans' mosques and madrasas; the Black Death of 1348; the Cairo Geniza; Isma'il's Downtown; Tahrir Square
facts.today: Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt, with a metropolitan area of more than 22 million people.

t: Cairo grew from a chain of settlements, Babylon Fortress, Fustat, al-Askar and al-Qata'i, until the Fatimids built al-Qahira in 969 as a palace city and the later rulers opened it to the public.
Under the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad the city reached close to half a million people by 1340, then lost many in the Black Death and in the shift of the spice trade to the Cape route.
Under the Ottomans Cairo became a provincial capital, and under Muhammad Ali and Isma'il it was rebuilt in part on European lines, becoming the capital of modern Egypt.
dyk: In 1168 the Fatimid vizier Shawar set fire to Fustat so that the Crusader king Amalric could not take it. The fire did not destroy the city, but it began its decline, and Cairo took over its trade.
ev: Amr ibn al-As founds Fustat beside Babylon Fortress after the Muslim conquest
The Fatimids conquer Egypt and Jawhar al-Saqili founds the city that becomes Cairo
Power passes from the Ayyubids to the Mamluks
The Black Death strikes the city
The Ottomans conquer Egypt and Cairo becomes a provincial capital
The Cairo Fire destroys nearly 700 shops, cinemas, casinos and hotels in the Downtown

sections.origins:
The land around Cairo lies where the Nile Valley meets the Delta, roughly the junction of Upper and Lower Egypt, on the routes between North Africa and the Levant. Memphis, the capital of Egypt in the Old Kingdom and a major city until the Ptolemaic period, stood a short distance south west of the present city. Heliopolis, an important religious centre, lay in what are now Matariya and Ain Shams in the north east. The Persian invasions of 525 BCE and 343 BCE largely destroyed it, and it was partly abandoned by the late first century BCE.

The origins of the modern city are generally traced to settlements of the first millennium CE. The trading post of Babylon, first mentioned in 50 BCE, became a fortress built by the emperor Diocletian (r. 285 to 305) at the entrance of a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea that Trajan (r. 98 to 117) had created. North of it was a port and outpost called Tendunyas or Umm Dunayn. Its bishop, Cyrus, took part in the Second Council of Ephesus in 449. The Byzantine-Sassanian War of 602 to 628 caused hardship and probably led much of the urban population to leave for the countryside. The oldest surviving churches, among them Saint Barbara and Saints Sergius and Bacchus, stand inside the fortress walls in what is now Old Cairo, or Coptic Cairo.
sections.growth:
Under the Fatimids Fustat reached its greatest size and prosperity as a centre of craftsmanship, international trade and the area's main Nile port. Sources report multi-storey communal residences there, some of seven floors and housing 200 to 350 people. Cairo itself remained a relatively exclusive royal city for most of the period. Under the vizier Badr al-Gamali (1073 to 1094) richer families from Fustat were first allowed to move in, and between 1087 and 1092 he rebuilt the walls in stone and raised the gates of Bab al-Futuh, Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuweila, which still stand. The Citadel, begun by Saladin in 1176, ended the palace city's exclusiveness and opened it to ordinary Egyptians and foreign merchants.

Under the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad (1293 to 1341, with interregnums) Cairo reached its apogee in population and wealth. By 1340 it had close to half a million people, making it the largest city west of China. Rental apartment buildings called rab' became common, and the Mamluks built mosques, madrasas and caravanserais that pushed the city outward. Under the Ottomans it was the second-largest city of the empire, after Constantinople, and spread south and west of the Citadel. Between 1882 and 1937 its population more than tripled, from 347,000 to 1.3 million, and its area grew from 10 to 163 square kilometres. Greater Cairo went from 2,986,280 people in 1947 to 16,292,269 in 2006.
sections.rulers:
After the Muslim conquest of Egypt (639 to 642), led by Amr ibn al-As, Fustat became the administrative capital. In 750, after the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, they laid out al-Askar, a military-style camp, to the northeast as the provincial capital. In 870 Ahmad ibn Tulun, sent to Egypt in 868 with his stepfather Bakbak, founded al-Qata'i as his capital and by 878 was de facto independent ruler of Egypt and Syria. His dynasty, the Tulunids, was short-lived: in 905 the Abbasids sent a general to reassert direct control and razed al-Qata'i, except for the mosque.

In 969 the Fatimids conquered Egypt from Ifriqiya, and al-Mu'izz made the new city his capital in 973. In 1169 Saladin, nephew of the Zengid general Shirkuh, became vizier, and two years later he seized power from the family of the last Fatimid caliph, al-'Adid, founding the Ayyubid dynasty and aligning Egypt with the Sunni Abbasids of Baghdad. From 1250 to 1517 the Mamluks held the throne, passing it from one mamluk to another, generally without heredity and often violently. In 1517 the Ottoman sultan Selim I made Egypt a province with Cairo as its capital. After the French occupation (1798 to 1801), Muhammad Ali Pasha became viceroy in 1805 and ruled until his death in 1848. Britain held the country from 1882, and Egypt became independent in 1922.
sections.life:
Cairo became a centre of learning under the Fatimids. The al-Azhar mosque, commissioned during the building of the city, developed into a university, and the library of Cairo held hundreds of thousands of books. Under the Ottomans al-Azhar attained a predominance among Islamic schools that it still holds. Cairo has been the seat of the Coptic Orthodox Church since the 12th century. Benjamin of Tudela reported 7,000 Jews there in 1170, and the Cairo Geniza, almost 200,000 Jewish manuscripts written from about 870 to 1880, was found in the Ben Ezra Synagogue of Fustat, built in 882, and in other places.

Housing was organised in close-knit neighbourhoods called harat, whose gates could be closed at night or in disturbances. Trade was housed in caravanserais, the wikalas and khans. Khan el-Khalili dates to 1385, when Amir Jarkas el-Khalili built a large caravanserai, which Sultan al-Ghuri rebuilt in the early 16th century. In the 16th and 17th centuries Cairo carried Yemeni coffee and Indian textiles to Anatolia, North Africa and the Balkans, and its merchants supplied the Hejaz during the hajj. The first printing press in the Middle East, printing in Hebrew, was set up in Cairo c. 1557; it is known only from two fragments in the Geniza. At the end of the 18th century twenty percent of the population were religious minorities and foreigners from around the Mediterranean.
sections.crises:
In 1168 the Fatimid vizier Shawar set fire to the unfortified Fustat to keep it from Amalric, the Crusader king of Jerusalem. The fire did not destroy the city, but it marked the beginning of its decline. When Ibn Battuta returned in 1348 the Black Death was ravaging most major cities, and he cited reports of thousands of deaths a day in Cairo. The plague struck the city more than fifty times between 1348 and 1517. In its first and deadliest waves about 200,000 people died, and by the 15th century the population had fallen to between 150,000 and 300,000. Political instability lasted from 1348 to 1412. The city's role in trade was diminished by Vasco da Gama's sea route round the Cape of Good Hope, between 1497 and 1499, which let spice traders avoid it.

Napoleon reached Cairo in 1798, when the population was under 300,000, forty percent lower than at the height of Mamluk influence in the mid-14th century. British and Ottoman forces besieged the city, and the French surrendered on 22 June 1801. The 1952 riots known as the Cairo Fire, or Black Saturday, destroyed nearly 700 shops, cinemas, casinos and hotels in the Downtown. An earthquake in 1992 caused 545 deaths, injured 6,512 and left about 50,000 homeless. In the revolution of 2011, which began in Tahrir Square on 25 January, at least 846 people were killed and 6,000 injured; Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February.
sections.legacy:
Cairo holds one of the largest concentrations of historical Islamic monuments in the world: the Mosque of Ibn Tulun, built in 876 to 879 and the oldest mosque that keeps its original form; the Fatimid gates and mosques; the Madrasa-Mosque of Sultan Hasan, the largest Mamluk religious monument; and the Mamluk complexes of Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad and Barquq. Its historic centre was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The Citadel was the seat of government and residence of its rulers until 1874, when Khedive Isma'il moved to 'Abdin Palace. Isma'il's Downtown, with its squares and boulevards, was inspired by the ideas of Baron Haussmann. The Nilometer on Roda Island, of the 860s, is the oldest surviving Islamic-era structure in the city.

The King Fuad edition of the Qur'an, published in Cairo on 10 July 1924, has become the standard for much modern printing. Since 1952 the city has expanded by new towns in the desert and by informal housing: by 2009 over 63 percent of Greater Cairo's people lived in informal neighbourhoods on 17 percent of its area. In 2015 plans were announced for a new administrative capital east of the city. Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt; the 2017 census counted 9,539,673 people in the city, and the metropolitan area has more than 22 million.

summary: Cairo grew out of Babylon Fortress and Fustat, and the Fatimids founded the city proper in 969. It was the Mamluk capital at its height, with close to half a million people by 1340, an Ottoman provincial centre, and then, from the 19th century, the rebuilt capital of modern Egypt.
notes: Disagreement inside the article: the history section says Cairo was founded in 969 (built over four years, the caliph arriving in 973), but the Islamic Cairo section says the Fatimid army founded it in 959 AD. I used 969 and left 959 out.
The Nilometer on Roda Island is dated 861 in the history section and 862 in the Islamic Cairo section; I wrote 'of the 860s'.

Al-Azhar: the history section says it was commissioned during the four years of building (before 973); the Islamic Cairo section says it was founded in 970. I wrote only that it was commissioned during the building of the city.
The lead says the Giza pyramid complex, Memphis and Heliopolis are 'today within the city'; elsewhere the article says Giza is a separate city on the west bank. I left Giza out.

The article says Tendunyas lay 'near al-Azbakiya'; left out. The article's Amr ibn al-As mosque founding year (642) and Fustat founding ('641 or early 642') differ slightly; I used '641 or 642' for Fustat.
The conquest is given as 639 to 642, Babylon besieged September 640, fell April 641; I used only the span.

Population: 'close to half a million' in 1340 is the article's wording; the 150,000 to 300,000 range for the 15th century and 'less than 300,000' in 1798 are as given. Present-day figures: lead says more than 9.8 million in the city and over 22 million in Greater Cairo; the 2017 census gives 9,539,673. I used the census figure and the lead's 22 million.

Left out by design: economy, transport, sport, pollution, traffic, women's rights, climate, the new capital's details beyond the 2015 announcement. Events since 1952 are the Cairo Fire, the 1992 earthquake and 2011, told without verdict; the article says nothing on 1956 to 2011 politics apart from Nasser's rebuilding.

Wanted but not found in the article: Muhammad Ali's reforms in Cairo beyond the title 'founder of modern Egypt' and the Citadel mosque; Isma'il's Suez Canal date (only 'the opening of the Suez Canal'); the Mamluk sultans' dates for the Black Death beyond the 1348 return of Ibn Battuta; the fate of Fatimid palaces beyond land being sold under Ayyubids and Mamluks; Napoleon's dates in Cairo; what happened to Cairo in the 1919 revolution beyond demonstrations.
